title: The caching flip: the bigger prompt is now the cheaper prompt — agentic cost is a harness-design property, not a model-price choice
summary: New evidence is inverting a decade of 'trim your prompts to save money' intuition. The arXiv study 'Don't Break the Cache' shows that in long-horizon agent loops the dominant cost driver is structural: naive agents re-serialize and re-inject the entire history every turn, so token cost grows quadratically with session length. Exact-prefix prompt caching collapses that curve toward linear and cuts input-token costs by up to ~90% (practitioner reports put API savings at 41–80%), and since agentic sessions run 20–25x more input than output tokens, this is where the bill actually lives. The counterintuitive corollary: a larger, stable cached prefix is often cheaper than a lean, churning one, because every reformat or aggressive context compaction is a cache reset that forces full recomputation. The insight for engineering leaders: the biggest cost lever in agentic coding is not switching to a cheaper model — it is harness and context-engineering discipline (stable prefixes, cache-aware tools, compaction timed 'like a database vacuum'). Two teams on the identical model can see an order-of-magnitude cost gap purely from loop design, which means cost optimization is an in-house engineering capability, not just a procurement decision.
source: arXiv Preprint ('Don't Break the Cache: An Evaluation of Prompt Caching for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks'), with corroborating practitioner analyses
whyItMatters: The dominant driver of agentic bills is loop architecture (quadratic context re-injection), not headline per-token price — so the highest-ROI cost work is engineering the harness, not renegotiating the model.
Old 'trim the prompt' advice is now actively counterproductive: a stable, well-cached large prefix can be cheaper and better-performing than a lean prompt that keeps breaking the cache.

Because two teams on the same model can differ ~10x on cost through loop design, cost efficiency becomes an internal engineering competency and a real differentiator, not merely a vendor-selection outcome.
Context compaction — which many agents (and defaults) trigger automatically near context limits — silently resets the cache and can spike cost; it needs to be timed and governed, not left implicit.
recommendedActions: Instrument cache-hit rate and input-token cost per agent session as first-class metrics, not just total spend.
Design harnesses for stable, append-only context prefixes and cache-aware tool ordering; avoid per-turn reformatting that invalidates the cache.
Treat context compaction as a deliberate, timed operation (like a DB vacuum) with measured cost/benefit, rather than an automatic trigger at the context ceiling.
Before switching models to save money, run a caching/context-engineering pass on the existing harness — it is often the larger and faster win.
risksAndCaveats: Caching economics depend on provider implementations (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google differ), cache TTLs, and request routing across replicas, so realized savings vary and can erode if traffic patterns break prefix reuse.
Caching reduces the linear re-processing term but does not eliminate the underlying quadratic growth of accumulating context, so very long horizons still need genuine context management.
Some cost-reduction percentages come from practitioner/vendor sources and specific workloads; absolute savings should be validated on your own agent traces.
